title: A 1998-2020 farmland-versus-forest heat contrast in US NestWatch nest success did not repeat in 2021-2025 nests and depended on the habitat code and heat measure
abstract: Lauck et al. (2023) reported that hot weather during nesting decreased NestWatch nest success in agricultural land and increased it in forest in 1998-2020. We rebuilt their variables from NestWatch Open Dataset version 6 and gridMET: success means at least one fledgling, land use comes from the habitat code at the nest, and heat is the 46-day maximum Tmax z-score against 1980-2000. We fitted logistic models with species, year and region fixed effects. We then applied the same method to 76,398 nests from 2021-2025 that the original study did not use. In 160,946 nests from 1998-2020, we found the published pattern: the agriculture slope was -0.070 logit per SD (SE 0.032), the forest slope +0.046 (SE 0.021) and the contrast -0.116 (SE 0.039). The contrast stayed negative with region-by-year, site and observer controls, nest-discovery filters, outcome-code filters and location-precision filters. In 2021-2025, the contrast was +0.085 (SE 0.080). The difference between periods was +0.201 (SE 0.089, p = 0.023). The contrast was negative in all five earlier year blocks and positive in both later blocks. Within 1998-2020, the contrast was absent with the 100-m habitat code (-0.014, SE 0.031) or with the 46-day mean temperature (-0.026, SE 0.039). It was mostly western (-0.295 west of 100 W, -0.062 east). Developed sites had negative heat slopes in both periods. Limitations: the forward period is short and had 31% power for a significant negative contrast of the earlier size. We used fixed-effect models, not the authors' GLMM, and did not add land-cover proportion covariates. NestWatch lay dates are often estimated, and the outcome does not use exposure days. NestWatch data are CC BY-NC and are not bundled; code, aggregate results, hashes and a retrieval script are included.
